conclusions.title: Why HY4 prefill reaches only 1.48M uncached TPM
conclusions.summary: The low rate is reproducible in standalone prefill. HY4 is spending substantial GPU time on the sink-compatible 128-head BF16 sparse-attention path, attention buffer operations, iHC, an additional attention gate, and an FP32 MoE router. Pipeline communication/waiting adds visible residency. A 15% useful-FLOP difference omits these implementation and precision costs; it cannot predict the observed 2.27× throughput gap. This profile identifies concrete optimization targets, but does not experimentally apportion the entire historical GLM–HY4 gap.

findings.title: 1.48M is reproducible without Decode or P→D transfer
findings.detail: Original HY4 capacity was 1,479,319.78 uncached tokens/minute versus historical GLM 3,357,505.96 (2.270×). A new capture-inactive control reached 1,459,572.09; the profiled run reached 1,490,701.85. Each completed the same 128 source requests, concurrency 80, one output token, with zero request errors and zero Decode batches. This standalone run has no Dynamo frontend, P→D transfer, or Mooncake remote storage in its request path. Both phases began after warmup and four-rank cache flush. Cache outcomes differ by 2,240 tokens, so these are close reproductions rather than identical execution schedules.

findings.title: Useful FLOPs are +15.05%, not a latency budget
findings.detail: The public ledger exactly recomputes from the deployed model config: HY4 12.5930 PF versus GLM 10.9453 PF for one fully uncached 100K causal prompt, +15.0543%. That ledger excludes memory movement, casts, indexing/top-k, physical padding, communication and launch/queue cost. The measured replay instead uses 8K chunks with cache prefixes and multiple prompt lengths. Also, NVFP4 applies to routed experts; the attention path, shared expert, router and first dense layer are not all FP4. Naively dividing GLM throughput by 1.15054 yields 2.92M, but assumes equal execution efficiency and workload and is not a measured achievable target.

findings.title: Largest computation kernel: sink-compatible sparse attention padded 64 → 128
findings.detail: All 50,700 layer forwards use the head128 sparse-attention kernel although HY4 has 64 useful attention heads. Actual source requires 128-head alignment on Blackwell and pads the query; the selected backend is BF16 flashmla_sparse to support learned attention sinks. Its raw device-summed kernel residency is 170.881 s, 27.11% of 630.345 s non-NCCL residency. The historical GLM startup instead selected DSA/TRT-LLM. This is the leading backend optimization target. The trace does not prove that removing padding halves kernel latency, and sinks must be preserved.
evidence: exact CUDA-launch/NVTX attn_mqa ownership for 50700 events

findings.title: Query-head padding alone adds 8.18% of non-NCCL residency
findings.detail: For every layer forward, the BF16 query is materialized as 128 heads: 50,700 large copy kernels consume 34.6626 device-summed seconds and 50,700 fills consume 16.8987 seconds. Together they cost 51.5613 seconds, 8.18% of non-NCCL kernel residency, in addition to the sparse-attention kernel itself. For a full 8K chunk, the padded query allocation is 1.208 GB and the 64-head copy writes 0.604 GB; these are tensor sizes, not measured DRAM traffic. Another 50,700 small attention copies total only 0.2035 seconds; these make k_rope contiguous before KV-cache insertion and are not query padding. The output trim is a view; it is not the large copy. A compatible 64-head kernel could avoid both the padded work and this materialization, but its actual speedup remains unmeasured.

findings.title: HY4-specific gate/iHC remain material despite existing fusions
findings.detail: The HPC attention-output gate consumes47.635 device-summed seconds (7.56% of non-NCCL residency). HPC iHC pre/post/post-pre/head kernels consume 62.233 s (9.87%). These paths are already fused and enabled; missing fusion flags are not the finding. The extra gate contributes useful arithmetic, while iHC can be expensive relative to its arithmetic count because it touches the expanded residual state. These are measured costs within HY4, not an isolated causal delta against a GLM kernel trace.

findings.title: The MoE router runs FP32 SIMT GEMM
findings.detail: All 50,050 FP32 SIMT SGEMM-family kernels are launched inside layers.N.mlp.gate: 26.663 device-summed seconds (4.23% of non-NCCL residency). This is distinct from the HPC attention gate. NVFP4 routed-expert GEMMs do not make the router, shared expert, or attention path FP4. Any router precision/kernel change needs routing and output correctness checks; no such change was made.

findings.title: Pipeline waiting is visible; batches are full and all four stages run
findings.detail: 649 of 650 profiled logical batches contain 8192 new tokens; the last has 6272. Each PP rank executes 650 model forwards and every one of 78 layers appears 650 times. Across the 214.123 s kernel window, non-NCCL interval union is 153.37–160.47 s per GPU; NCCL coverage not overlapped by other kernels is 51.41–58.50 s per GPU (about 24–27% of the window). This NCCL residency can include waiting for a peer as well as transfer, so it is not proof of saturated NVLink or a measured critical path. Non-NCCL kernels run concurrently on at least 3 GPUs for 152.60 s. PP async depth 1 means 5 logical loop slots for PP4, not one serial slot. Average non-NCCL coverage per logical batch is 236.85, 235.96, 246.87 and 245.90 ms across the four stages: only 4.63% max/min imbalance. This supports broad stage cost rather than one overwhelmingly slow rank. Representative steps 301–303 on PP0 and PP3 were reviewed; no dependency-release timestamps establish a critical path.

findings.title: CUDA graphs do not explain the historical difference
findings.detail: Recovered original GLM logs show all 8310 formal batches per rank with CUDA graphs False, despite the old public page describing the configured breakable graph mode. HY4 graphs are also off. GLM PP async depth 0 gives 4 logical loop slots; HY4 depth 1 gives 5. Neither the public graph configuration statement nor the numeric depth alone supports a causal explanation.

limitations: These are device-summed kernel residency shares, not wall-time shares, useful FLOPs, SM utilization, MFU or achievable speedups. Overlap and dependency waiting are retained and audited separately.

The historical GLM run used GB300/Grace, a different software image, corpus/tokenizer, context distribution, cache policy and backend. No historical GLM kernel trace was recovered. The exact 2.27× gap has not been causally decomposed by a matched A/B experiment.
The 128-request diagnostic phases have colder aggregate cache outcomes and a finite tail; they reproduce throughput but do not replace the original 10-minute capacity qualification.
Current B300 power-limit flags were active with no thermal-limit flags in sampled observations. Historical GB300 clocks/power were not recovered, so hardware contribution is unquantified.

The profiler stop HTTP request timed out after all request EOFs. Native finalization later completed on all four ranks, and a separately hashed export/coverage receipt qualifies this analysis. The original control failure is preserved.
next_steps: Prioritize a sink-correct sparse-attention kernel that supports 64 useful heads without 128-head padding; test exact output/sink behavior and replay the same bounded input before claiming a gain.

Remove avoidable query-padding allocation/fill/copy where kernel contracts permit. The existing q8 backend explicitly rejects non-null attention sinks, so it cannot simply replace this HY4 path; retain sink semantics in any implementation.
Profile and optimize the already-enabled HPC gate/iHC paths and FP32 router; preserve checkpoint semantics and routing correctness.
Evaluate PP scheduling or stage balance only with a controlled same-workload A/B and dependency-aware timeline; NCCL residence alone does not establish a network bottleneck.
For a numeric explanation of the entire historical gap, capture GLM and HY4 on the same hardware/software generation with matched chunk, context and cache-work distributions.
